column4: The rabbis and scholars judge by the Torah because they were entrusted with preserving Allah's Book; this states the section's image of written revelation deposited for human custody.
Allah writes admonition and detailed instruction for Moses on the tablets, then tells him to take them firmly; writing, reminder, and active holding coincide.
When Moses takes up the tablets, their inscription contains guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord, joining written custody to the fearing recipient of reminder.
The man who forgot Joseph in 12:42 remembers after a long interval and offers to transmit the needed interpretation; this completes forgetting with recovery and report.
After the former generations, Allah gives Moses the Book as insight, guidance, and mercy so that people may remember; earlier time, Mosaic writing, and recollection meet explicitly.
The Prophet's wives are told to remember what is recited in their houses of Allah's signs and wisdom, directly linking oral recital with deliberate retention.
عَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ gives Allah the direct role of teaching the Quran, a close counterpart to the causative “We shall make you recite.”
The command to recite whatever is easy of the Quran, repeated within the ayah, explicitly joins recitation to divinely recognized ease.
Immediately after the divine gathering and recitation passage, the hearers are said to love the immediate life, continuing directly into the preference diagnosed at 87:16.
The hearers leave the Hereafter while loving the immediate life in 75:20; this supplies the other half of the same near-versus-lasting choice.
Each soul receives what it earned, and believers pray not to be held accountable if they forget or err; personal share and human forgetting occur together as in the contents of the earlier pages.
The present Book comes in truth, confirming prior scripture and serving as its guardian; the verse defines continuity and custody across the gathered prophetic writings.
Allah sends the best discourse as a harmonious, repeated Book; bodies react and hearts soften to Allah's remembrance, joining articulated text, repetition, and received dhikr.

Believers are summoned to let their hearts respond to the Reminder and truth, unlike earlier recipients of the Book whose hearts hardened over time; it stages retention and loss across scriptural history.
A good word is compared to a good tree with a firm root and high branches, giving a nonlexical image of speech that is held rather than dropped.
The good word's tree continually gives fruit by its Lord's permission, showing what a firmly retained word goes on producing.
A corrupt word is like a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, a precise reversal of the section's gathered and securely held word.
Allah makes believers firm through the firm word in this life and the Hereafter, naming divine stabilization as the reason the word does not fall away.
Worldly possessions are passing enjoyment and adornment, while what is with Allah is better and more enduring; the wording closely parallels the choice in 87:16-17.
What people receive is enjoyment of worldly life, whereas what is with Allah is better and more enduring for believers, another direct formulation of the section's value contrast.
Those who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter are identified by that preference, directly restating the stance criticized at 87:16.
Disbelief is explained by preferring worldly life over the Hereafter, another explicit boundary between the passing and enduring objects of choice.
The rejecters love the immediate life and leave behind a weighty Day, closely repeating the near-life preference and its neglected lasting consequence.
No bearer bears another's burden and every soul earns only against itself, repeating the first teaching quoted from the pages in 53:38.
No burdened soul bears another's burden, independently repeating the teaching preserved in the Mosaic and Abrahamic pages.
No burdened soul can carry another's burden, even when a heavily laden person calls for help; the ayah expands the earlier pages' teaching with a concrete boundary.
No bearer bears another's burden, again preserving across the Quran the teaching identified as content of the first pages.
A group twists its tongues with the Book so listeners think the utterance belongs to the Book when it does not; oral delivery is severed from its written source.
People write a book with their own hands and falsely call it from Allah, a direct counterfeit of divinely given words gathered into authentic pages.
Some listen to the Prophet but immediately ask what he just said after leaving; this is a concrete, nonlexical failure to hold received speech.
If the sea were ink for the Lord's words, the sea would run out before those words did; material inscription cannot exhaust the speech it tries to gather.
Even all trees as pens and seas as ink would not exhaust Allah's words, setting a limit on pages while affirming the inexhaustibility of divine speech.
Israel is told to hold firmly what it was given and listen, but answers with hearing and disobedience; reception without faithful custody reverses the intended holding.
Those given the Book recite it with its true recitation, presenting faithful reading as the proper handling of an entrusted scripture.
Abraham asks for a messenger who will recite God's signs and teach the Book, anticipating the movement from divinely supplied utterance to learned scripture.
The sent messenger recites signs, purifies, and teaches the Book and wisdom, describing the public transmission that follows the Prophet's receipt of recitation.
The messenger recites signs and teaches the Book to a people formerly astray, repeating the prophetic chain from received words to taught writing.
Jesus follows earlier prophets with the Gospel, confirming the Torah and providing guidance and admonition, showing revelation retained and relayed across successive books.
The unlettered Messenger is found described in the Torah and Gospel, a specific instance of present prophetic reality preserved in earlier writings.
Those who read the Book before the Prophet are named as witnesses to prior revelation, linking present recitation with an older community of readers.
What people possess runs out while what is with Allah remains, stating the passing-versus-retained relation that the section makes perceptible through memory and pages.
The skeptics demand that a book descend for them to read, a physicalized demand for revelation comparable to the opened pages demanded in 74:52.
Allah makes the revelation easy on the Prophet's tongue for glad tidings and warning, a vocal counterpart to the promise of facilitated recitation.
Turning away from Allah's Reminder leads to a constricted life and blindness at resurrection, establishing the rejected reminder whose forgotten signs are named in 20:126.
The raised person asks why he is blind although he once saw; this question lets 20:126 explain that forgotten signs yield a corresponding abandonment.
“This is the Reminder of those with me and those before me” places present and earlier communities' revelation under the single category of dhikr.
The worldly life is only temporary enjoyment while the Hereafter is the lasting abode, a direct thematic restatement of the preference boundary.
Allah makes the revelation an Arabic Quran so people may understand, supplying the articulated recitation whose written heavenly locus is named in 43:4.
Every community is summoned to its Book for judgment, setting the scene for the divinely copied record that speaks in 45:29.
Allah's Book speaks truth because human deeds were being copied into it, another concrete mechanism by which what passes is retained in writing.
The believers bear an أَثَر of prostration on their faces and have corresponding portrayals in the Torah and Gospel; visible trace and earlier scriptural witness meet in one ayah.
After teaching the Quran in 55:2, Allah teaches the human being clear expression, completing the move from received revelation to articulated speech.
The Messenger recites divine signs and teaches the Book among the unlettered, a public continuation of the divinely enabled recitation promised to the Prophet.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from Allah's remembrance, specifying worldly attachment as a cause of lost dhikr.
The oath by the pen and what people inscribe foregrounds the material act by which spoken or known content becomes lasting writing.
